### Source-grounded content

Enterococcus species

Enterococcus species isolates comprised of 10% of the annual AMR data and contributed to
46% of the Gram-positive cocci data reported during 2024 (Table 3). A total of 20,719
Enterococcus species isolates data was submitted by the NARS-Net sites of which 19,976
isolates were from unique patients (Fig. 2). Upon analysis of 19,976 unique patient isolates,
isolation rates from specimen types like urine, blood, pus aspirates and other sterile body fluids
were 68%, 18%, 10% and 4% respectively (Table 4). Among Enterococcus species isolated from
blood, highest resistance was observed to erythromycin 79% (CI: 77.3- 80.2) and Ampicillin
(71%, CI: 69.4-72.7) (Table 7). Notably resistance to vancomycin (22%, CI: 20.9-23.8) and
teicoplanin (26%, CI: 24.4-27.9) is constantly increasing from last 3 years. Resistance to linezolid
(1.7%, CI: 1.3-2.2) among blood isolates is similar to last year’s report.
Among the urinary isolates, 58% were resistant to first-line antibiotic ampicillin (CI: 57.1 – 58.9)
and 53% to gentamicin-high (CI: 52.2-54.1). Highest resistance was observed to ciprofloxacin
(82%, CI: 81.1 - 82.8) and lowest was observed to linezolid 0.44 % (CI: 0.3-0.6). Resistance to
vancomycin among urinary isolates was higher than that in last year’s report (6% in 2023 to
12% in 2024) (Table 7).
Enterococcus spp. isolates from inpatient wards were almost double the outpatient patient
isolates which were in turn nearly twice the isolates from ICU patients. (Table 5). AST analysis
of blood isolates of Enterococcus spp. showed higher resistance to linezolid in isolates from
patients in intensive care units in comparison to those from inpatient wards and outpatient
clinics. (Fig. 9) Incidence of VRE among blood isolates is 24% in inpatients and 21% in ICU
settings. (Fig. 9) Higher vancomycin resistance was observed in blood isolates than in urinary
isolates (Fig. 9, 10). Among urinary isolates of Enterococcus species, 43% resistance was
observed to nitrofurantoin in ICU settings.

### Source-grounded content

1.2.3.2. Gram-Negative Bacilli

Seven Gram-Negative bacteria of public health importance are included under AMR
surveillance being coordinated at NARS-Net sites. These are Escherichia coli, Klebsiella species,
Pseudomonas species, Acinetobacter species, Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi and Paratyphi,
Shigella species and Vibrio cholerae. In the current report, 1,60,956 isolates of Gram-negative
bacilli have been reported from 1,51,192 unique patients which account for 78% of total priority
pathogens reported from 54 sentinel surveillance sites.

 1.2.3.2.1. Enterobacteriaceae

Data of 1,17,184 isolates of E. coli, Klebsiella species, Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi and
Paratyphi and Shigella species was submitted by network sites from 1,10,022 unique patients.
Enterobacteriaceae accounted for 56% of all the priority pathogens.

Escherichia coli

A total of 68,384 E. coli isolates were reported from 64,254 unique patients. E. coli contributed
to one-third of the unique patient AST data during the year 2024 (Fig. 2). E coli was most
commonly isolated from the urine samples (70%) followed by pus aspirate (21%), blood (6%)
and sterile body fluids (4%) respectively. (Table 4).
E. coli isolates showed more than 50% resistance to all the tested antibiotics except
carbapenems, colistin and aminoglycosides. The highest resistance was observed to ampicillin
as noted in previous years (Table 8). High proportion of resistance to ciprofloxacin was observed
ranging between 73% to 78% in all specimen types. Resistance to nitrofurantoin in urinary
isolates showed an increasing trend over last 3 years (increased from 9% in 2022 to 19% in
2024). (Table 8)
Amongst third generation cephalosporins tested, resistance ranging between 79% to 83% was
observed in all specimen types. β-lactam inhibitor combination i.e. amoxicillin-clavulanate also
had high resistance of 68% in blood isolates. Among carbapenems, ertapenem (49%) had
higher resistance rate than imipenem (40%) and meropenem (36%) in E. coli blood isolates
(Table 8). For colistin susceptibility testing, isolates tested using colistin agar screen and broth

### Source-grounded content

Klebsiella species

In the current data reporting period, 47,744 Klebsiella species isolates were reported of which
44,725 were from unique patients. The isolation rate of Klebsiella spp. in data reported by the
sentinel sites was highest from urine (46%) followed by pus aspirate (30%), blood (18%) and
OSBF (6%) (Table 4).
Blood isolates showed more than 50% resistance to all the tested antibiotics except for colistin.
Proportion of ESBL producing Klebsiella species from blood was higher (84%) than urinary
isolates (70%). Majority of carbapenemase producing Klebsiella species were isolated from
blood (55%-57%) followed by OSBF (46%-48%), pus aspirates (43%) and urine specimens (31%
- 32%). Two-third of the urinary isolates tested showed resistance to aminoglycosides (amikacin
and gentamycin,40%); whereas more than half of the blood isolates had resistance to
aminoglycosides (amikacin;60% and gentamycin; 55%) (Table 9). Approx. 50% of urinary
isolates showed resistance to nitrofurantoin.
 Resistance to the reserve antibiotic, colistin, was found to be highest in Klebsiella spp.
compared to other Gram-negative priority pathogens isolated from all the specimen types
which is similar to observations in previous year’s report. All colistin resistant isolates have been
confirmed at the AMR NRL at NCDC.
Location type wise AST data revealed higher resistance to all the tested antibiotics except
ertapenem and gentamicin in Klebsiella species isolated from blood of ICU patients compared
to the Klebsiella species isolated from inpatients and outpatients (Fig. 13). Among
carbapenems, ertapenem showed highest resistance (71%) followed by meropenem (61%) and
imipenem (57%) in blood isolates from ICU patients. Similarly, high resistance was observed to
third generation cephalosporins viz. cefotaxime (88%), cefuroxime (87%) and ceftriaxone (86%)
among blood isolates from intensive care units. Moreover, more than 60% resistance was
observed to the first line antibiotics. (Fig. 13). Fifty-five percent of Klebsiella spp. isolated from
blood showed resistance to imipenem and 57% were resistant to meropenem (Table 9).

Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi and Paratyphi
In the current reporting period, data of 975 Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi and Paratyphi
isolates was submitted to NCDC, of which 962 isolates were from unique patients. Twenty of
these isolates were from stool specimens. Data of 834 unique isolates of S. enterica Typhi and
108 isolates of S. enterica Paratyphi from blood has been analyzed . Among the first line
antibiotics, highest resistance was to ciprofloxacin (35%). Low resistance to other first-line
antibiotics like ampicillin (5%), chloramphenicol (2%) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
(5.3%) was observed. (Table 10) Ten isolates of S. enterica sero. Typhi were found to be resistant
to ceftriaxone, two isolates were resistant to azithromycin. Four isolates of ceftriaxone resistant
S. enterica serovar Paratyphi were observed during 2024. All the ceftriaxone resistant,
azithromycin resistant and imipenem resistant S. Typhi isolates included in this report were
confirmed at the AMR-NRL at NCDC.

1.2.3.2.2. Non-Fermenting Gram-Negative Bacilli

Among the non-fermenting Gram-Negative bacilli (NF GNB) included in the data submitted
during January-December 2024 from the NARS-Net sentinel surveillance sites, Pseudomonas
species was the most frequently isolated pathogen from 21,808 unique patients followed by
Acinetobacter species (19,122) (Fig 2). Among the NF GNB, Pseudomonas species was the
predominant isolate from inpatients, while Acinetobacter species was the predominant isolate
from patients in ICU settings (Table 5).

Pseudomonas species

In the current reporting year, surveillance sites submitted data of 23,255 isolates of
Pseudomonas spp. from 21,808 unique patients (Fig 2). Pseudomonas spp. isolates included in
the data during current reporting period were most commonly isolated from pus aspirate
(48%), urine (28%), blood (16%), and other sterile body fluids (8%) (Table 4).
Blood isolates of Pseudomonas species showed highest resistance (42%; CI: 39.8-43.4) to third-
generation cephalosporin (ceftazidime) followed by ciprofloxacin (29%; CI: 0.1-0.6) and
piperacillin-tazobactam (21%; CI: 20-23) among first line treatment agents for Pseudomonas
species. Similar resistance pattern was seen for pus aspirates and other sterile body fluids.
Among second line agents, resistance to imipenem was 36% (CI: 33.7-37.3) and aztreonam was
40% (CI: 37.9-42.2) (Table 12).
Among urinary isolates, 58% Pseudomonas spp. isolates were resistant to ciprofloxacin, 41% to
amikacin, and 32% to piperacillin-tazobactam. Approximately 40% of urinary isolates were
resistant to aztreonam (Table 12).
Among the reserve group of antibiotics namely colistin, five blood isolates (0.26%), two from
pus aspirate (0.038%), and four from urine (0.13%) were found to be resistant (Table 12).

1.2.3.2.2. Non-Fermenting Gram-Negative Bacilli

Among the non-fermenting Gram-Negative bacilli (NF GNB) included in the data submitted
during January-December 2024 from the NARS-Net sentinel surveillance sites, Pseudomonas
species was the most frequently isolated pathogen from 21,808 unique patients followed by
Acinetobacter species (19,122) (Fig 2). Among the NF GNB, Pseudomonas species was the
predominant isolate from inpatients, while Acinetobacter species was the predominant isolate
from patients in ICU settings (Table 5).

Pseudomonas species

In the current reporting year, surveillance sites submitted data of 23,255 isolates of
Pseudomonas spp. from 21,808 unique patients (Fig 2). Pseudomonas spp. isolates included in
the data during current reporting period were most commonly isolated from pus aspirate
(48%), urine (28%), blood (16%), and other sterile body fluids (8%) (Table 4).
Blood isolates of Pseudomonas species showed highest resistance (42%; CI: 39.8-43.4) to third-
generation cephalosporin (ceftazidime) followed by ciprofloxacin (29%; CI: 0.1-0.6) and
piperacillin-tazobactam (21%; CI: 20-23) among first line treatment agents for Pseudomonas
species. Similar resistance pattern was seen for pus aspirates and other sterile body fluids.
Among second line agents, resistance to imipenem was 36% (CI: 33.7-37.3) and aztreonam was
40% (CI: 37.9-42.2) (Table 12).

### Source-grounded content

Acinetobacter spp.

Data of a total of 20,276 Acinetobacter species isolates was submitted by network sites during
this reporting period of Jan – Dec 2024, of which 19,122 were from unique patients. Among all
specimen types under the programme, Acinetobacter species was most commonly isolated
from blood (39%) followed by pus aspirate (30%), urine (18%) and other sterile body fluids
(12%). (Table 4)
High level of resistance was observed to all the tested antibiotics including Minocycline in
isolates from blood, pus samples and other sterile body fluids. (Fig. 15) Blood isolates showed
the highest resistance to ceftazidime (82%; CI: 80.8- 82.8) followed by ampicillin-sulbactam
(71%; CI: 68.7-72.3). Alarmingly high level of resistance to second line antimicrobial agents viz.
imipenem (70%) and meropenem (66%) was observed among blood isolates. (Table 13) Sixty-
nine percent of isolates from pus samples and 68% from other sterile body fluids were resistant
to imipenem. Ten isolates from blood, one from OSBF, 4 each from pus aspirates and urine
were resistant to colistin. (Table 13)

Vibrio cholerae

confirmed at AMR-NRL has been analyzed. The highest resistance was observed to
trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (73%)and lowest resistance to chloramphenicol (0.95). (Table

### Source-grounded content

1.2.4. AMR Trends

AMR Surveillance Data from NARSNET sites has been analyzed over last 7 years from 2017 to
2024. During 2020 data reported was small in volume due to the COVID pandemic. Trend
analysis of MRSA isolated from blood showed slight decrease in MRSA proportion from 59%
(2021) to 56% (2024). (Fig. 16) This decrease in proportion of MRSA may be attributed to the
increase in data submitted by the network sites. Trend analysis of VRE isolated from blood
showed continuous increase from 2021 (11%) to 2024 (22%). (Fig. 18) Trend analysis for ESBL
producing E. coli from blood showed an increase over the last 4 years from 2021 (76%) to 2024
(81%). (Fig. 19) Similar trend was observed in blood isolates of ESBL producing Klebsiella spp.
which have shown consistently high level of resistance from 81% in 2021 to 84% in 2024. (Fig.
19) Moreover, 3-year trend analysis of carbapenemase producing E. coli, Klebsiella species and
Acinetobacter species has shown consistent increase. (Fig 21,22)

2. AMR Surveillance in Fungal pathogens
 2.1. Background of National Reference Laboratory for AMR in fungal
 pathogens.
 Under the National Programme on AMR Containment, the National Reference
 Laboratory (NRL) for antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in fungal pathogens has been
 established at Vallabhbhai Patel Chest Institute (VPCI), New Delhi.

 2.2. AMR surveillance of Candida species from bloodstream infections
 The National Reference Laboratory at VPCI during January 2024-December 2024
 received a total of 1074 Candida strains from blood stream infections from 28 NARS-Net
 laboratories (Annexure-1) for phenotypic and molecular characterization and
 generating the antifungal susceptibility profile under “National Programme on AMR
 Containment”.
 2.2.1. Methodology:
 a) Phenotypic characterization of Candida isolates: All the stains received at NRL
 were first screened on differential selective media CHROMagar Candida
 Medium.
 b) Molecular characterization: All strains were identified by Matrix-Assisted Laser
 Desorption/Ionization Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometry (MALDI-TOF) and by
 sequencing of internal transcribed spacer region (ITS) of ribosomal
 deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and of the D1/D2 domain of the large subunit
 ribosomal DNA in case a low or no identification was obtained by MALDI.
 c) Antifungal susceptibility testing (AFST): AFST was performed using the Clinical
 and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) broth microdilution method (BMD),
 following M27-A3/S4.31,32.6 The antifungals tested were amphotericin B,
 itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, 5-flucytosine, caspofungin,
 micafungin and anidulafungin. All antifungals were dissolved in Dimethyl
 sulfoxide (DMSO). Roswell Park Memorial Institute medium (RPMI) 1640
 medium with glutamine without bicarbonate buffered to pH 7 with 0.165 M 3-

2.3. Significant Findings
 The NRL for AMR in fungal pathogens was operational since January 2022. Over the
 years the number of isolates received at the NRL have increased due to more number
 of NARS-Net sites submitting the isolates. Total of 1074 Candida isolates from blood
 cultures were received during 2024 (Fig 23).

2.3.1. Details of yeast isolates characterized at NRL during 2024:
 Most common Candida species isolated from bloodstream infection was Candida
 tropicalis (34%) followed by Pichia kudriavzevii (14%), Candida albicans (9%), Candida
 parapsilosis (8%), Candida auris (8%) and Cyberlindnera jadanii (7%) (Fig 24). Non-
 albicans Candida (NAC) species dominate the distribution, highlighting the
 epidemiological shift from C. albicans (Table 15).

 Out of all the patients from whom yeast strains were isolated, 59% were male and 41% were
 female. Neonates and infants (<1 year) accounted for the majority of isolates (54%) (Fig 25).
 The remaining age groups each contribute 4–6% of total isolates.

2.3.3. Location wise distribution of isolates:
 The distribution of fungal isolates across healthcare settings showed distinct patterns among
 different yeast species (Table 16). Majority of the candidemia cases were from the neonatal
 intensive care unit (NICU) (29%) and 7% were from the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU).
 Candida tropicalis and P. kudriavzevii were the most commonly isolated species, with C.
 tropicalis being particularly prevalent in intensive care unit (ICU; 55%) and inpatient
 departments (27%) settings, while P. kudriavzevii was most common in ICUs (71%),
 indicating its growing clinical importance in critical care (Table 16). C. auris, a known
 multidrug-resistant species, was primarily found in ICU (60%) and inpatient wards (18%).
 Candida albicans showed a strong presence in ICU (45%) and was also isolated notably from
 inpatients (35%). Other species like C. parapsilosis and C. glabrata were also found mainly in
 ICU. Interestingly, less common species like Cyberlindnera jadinii and Wickerhamomyces
 anomalus were predominantly isolated from patients in ICUs. Overall, the ICUs accounted
 for the highest proportion of isolates for most species, highlighting critical care units as a
 major hub for opportunistic fungal infections (Table 16).

Pichia kudriavzevii:
The antifungal susceptibility pattern of P. kudriavzevii (n=115) reveals a low resistance to
anidulafungin and micafungin, with resistance of approximately 2%. P. kudriavzevii is
intrinsically resistant to fluconazole. All other antifungal agents, including amphotericin B,
5-fluorocytosine, itraconazole, posaconazole, and voriconazole showed negligible or no
resistance.
Candida albicans:
The resistance analysis of C. albicans (n=71) shows notable resistance to fluconazole (8%;
MIC, ≥8 mg/L). A low rate of resistance (2%) was observed for micafungin (MIC, ≥1 mg/L),
while all other antifungal agents including amphotericin B, anidulafungin, 5-fluorocytosine,
itraconazole, posaconazole, and voriconazole exhibited good activity against all C. albicans
isolates (Fig 28).

### Source-grounded content

3. Discussion
This report is the eighth annual report of the National AMR Surveillance Network (NARS-Net).
This report includes 2,06,745 isolates AST data submitted by 54 sites. Like the previous year's
findings, one-third of the pathogens in the AMR Surveillance data for 2024 were Escherichia
coli (33%). Amongst the urinary isolates, E. coli (51%) was the most commonly isolated priority
pathogen, and urine was the most common specimen type (45%). As consistent with previous
reports, S. aureus was most commonly isolated from pus aspirates (66%). Klebsiella species was
most commonly isolated pathogen from urine (46%) and pus samples (30%).
Quality of AMR surveillance data submitted by the NARSNET sites has been ensured by
continuous hands-on laboratory and data management trainings, site support visits, monthly
data quality monitoring and feedback calls, and annual review meetings. EQAS program and
confirmation of Alert isolates at AMR-NRL, CBDDR, NCDC also played an essential role in
improving data quality of NARS-Net sites. Moreover, many of the sites are strictly performing
internal quality control of media, antibiotic discs as per recommendations under the
programme.
Compared to the previous year, the number of sites submitting data has increased from 41 to
54 sites situated in 33 states/UTs. Quality of colistin susceptibility testing has improved over
the years, as 44 of 54 sentinel sites have standardized and started performing colistin agar
dilution and colistin broth microdilution (BMD) tests. The wet lab trainings on broth
microdilution for the remaining 10 labs has been done by AMR-NRL at NCDC.
The AMR surveillance data in the current report like previous years continues to have the
limitation of samples for culture and sensitivity being referred only for patients requiring
admission and often not responding to the first line of antibiotics. This limitation has the
potential to skew the AMR trends to higher side than the actual trends.
Trend analysis for ESBL producing E. coli from blood showed an increase (2024; 81%) over the
last 3 years (2021; 76%) (Fig. 21). This may be attributed to higher usage of third generation

There has been a gradual increase in the proportion of Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus

isolated from blood over the past 5 years showed a slight decrease from 59% (2021) to 56%
(2024). (Fig 16). Among MRSA from blood specimens, highest resistance was observed to
erythromycin (77%) followed by ciprofloxacin (67%) and clindamycin (53%).

### Source-grounded content

A major observation of AMR surveillance for fungal pathogens is the predominance of NAC
species in bloodstream infections, with C. tropicalis being the most frequently isolated (34%),
followed by P. kudriavzevii (14%). C. albicans occurrence was found to be 9% followed by C.
parapsilosis (8%). This shift from C. albicans, which historically dominated invasive candidiasis,
reflects a broader global trend likely influenced by antifungal exposure and changing host
demographics. High proportion of isolates from neonates (29%) is particularly noteworthy and
points to their increased susceptibility to Candida infections due to underdeveloped immunity,
frequent use of invasive devices, and prolonged stays in NICUs. Overall, most isolates across
species were recovered from ICUs especially from NICU settings, underlining critical care
environments as high-risk reservoirs for opportunistic yeast infections. The antifungal
susceptibility patterns revealed fluconazole resistance in several species, most notably C. auris
(66%), C. parapsilosis (16%), W. anomalus (15%), C. albicans (8%), and C. tropicalis (7%).
Although resistance to amphotericin B, itraconazole and 5-fluorocytosine remained low,
emerging resistance to echinocandins in some species is concerning. These findings underscore
the necessity for routine species-level identification and susceptibility testing to guide
appropriate therapy. The presence of rare yeasts such as C. jadanii, Clavispora lusitaniae and
Trichosporon spp. further highlights the value of advanced diagnostic techniques in uncovering
uncommon pathogens. Overall, this data emphasizes the importance of continued antifungal
resistance monitoring, improved infection control practices in neonatal and ICU settings, and
the need to update empirical treatment protocols in light of evolving resistance patterns.
The AMR surveillance data presented in this report provides critical insights into resistance
trends and highlights areas needing focused attention. Strengthening surveillance systems,
addressing site-specific challenges and fostering inter-sectoral collaboration will be essential to

### Source-grounded content

Executive Summary

 Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) surveillance is crucial for tracking and combating the
growing threat of AMR. This is the ninth report of National AMR Surveillance Network (NARS-
Net) established under the National Programme on AMR Containment coordinated by the
National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), MoHFW, India. This report includes bacterial AMR
surveillance data from 62 sentinel surveillance sites. National programme on AMR containment
has been expanded in a phased manner and currently includes 70 laboratories in 34 states/UTs
(as of March 2026). This report provides insights into antimicrobial resistance patterns, trends
and emerging resistance across the network sites.

 The current report includes data of bacterial and fungal AMR Surveillance for the
reporting period from 01st January 2025 to 31st December 2025. Standard operating procedures
(SOPs) on antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), internal quality control (IQC), AMR data
management developed under the programme are implemented at NARS-Net sites to ensure
quality data. The panel of antimicrobials used for surveillance is standardized in alignment with
the international standards and prescription practices of clinicians in the country. Trainings and
workshops are conducted regularly for NARS-Net sites to ensure compliance to the SoPs under
the programme. Wet-lab trainings on colistin agar dilution, vancomycin screen agar and colistin
and vancomycin broth microdilution (BMD) testing, both at the NRL, NCDC and onsite during
site visits, have contributed to an increase in the number of sentinel sites performing MIC
determination and submitting quality data. Online trainings are also organized on regular basis
to reinforce the testing standards at laboratories. Monthly feedbacks through data quality
monitoring calls has played a crucial role in improving compliance to data standards defined
under the programme. Enrolment of sites under External Quality Assessment Scheme (EQAS)
and bacterial identification and AST confirmations of a defined number of isolates conducted
by AMR-NRLs, has played a significant role in improving data quality.

➢ Among the specimen types, urine (44%) was the most frequently reported specimen
 followed by pus aspirate (31%) and blood (18%). From urine specimens, E. coli (49%) was
 the most frequently isolated pathogen, while Klebsiella species was the most commonly
 isolated pathogen from blood specimens (25%) and Other sterile body fluids (26%) while
 from pus specimens Klebsiella species (24%) and S. aureus (23%) both were the predominant
 isolates.
➢ Majority of isolates of Enterococcus species were from urine specimens (68%) and most S.
 aureus isolates were from pus aspirates (67%) consistent with the previous reports.
➢ Proportion of MRSA in blood was slightly higher from last year in all settings, from 63% to
 65% in intensive care units, from 55% to 61% among inpatients and from 44% to 51% in
 outpatients.
➢ Proportion of VRE among blood isolates was found to be similar to that during last year, it
 was 20% in ICU setting and 19% among inpatients.
➢ Among E. coli from blood, 80% of isolates were ESBL producers, and among Klebsiella spp.
 blood isolates, 83% were ESBL producers.
➢ Also, trend analysis for carbapenem resistance in gram negative bacterial isolates from
 blood cultures showed a decreasing trend from previous year in E. coli (from 43% to 41%),
 Pseudomonas species (35% to 30%) and Acinetobacter species (70% to 68%) while
 carbapenem resistant Klebsiella spp. has slightly increased from 59% to 62%.

 This report emphasizes on the need for continuous strengthening of surveillance
system, targeted interventions, development of evidence-based policies, sustained
collaborations and investments to combat AMR. The AMR surveillance data in this report serves
as a crucial resource for policy makers, healthcare professionals, and researchers working to
address the growing threat of AMR.

### Source-grounded content

1. Bacterial AMR Surveillance

1.1. Introduction

 Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a rapidly escalating global health threat. As pathogens
evolve to resist the existing antimicrobials, once-manageable diseases become increasingly
difficult or impossible to cure. Global Burden of Disease 2021 report by Antimicrobial
Resistance Collaborators published in The Lancet (2024) estimated that 4.71 million deaths
were associated with bacterial AMR including 1.14 million deaths attributable to bacterial
AMR.1 The report also states that among Gram-negative bacteria, resistance to carbapenems
increased more than any other antibiotic class, rising from 0.619 million deaths in 1990 to 1.03
million associated deaths in 2021. The report also forecasted that an estimated 1.91 million
deaths attributable to AMR and 8.22 million deaths associated with AMR could occur globally
in 2050. These figures highlight the immense burden of AMR on public health, particularly in
low- and middle-income countries where access to quality healthcare and diagnostics is limited.
Beyond mortality, AMR also leads to prolonged illness, increased healthcare costs, and greater
risk of complications, posing a serious threat to modern medicine, including surgery, cancer
therapy and intensive care. Without urgent and coordinated action, AMR will continue to
undermine modern medicine and threaten global health security. To monitor AMR, a robust
surveillance system is needed in the global fight against drug-resistant infections, providing the
critical data needed to track resistance patterns, update treatment guidelines, and guide public
health interventions.

 To address the problem of AMR, Government of India initiated the National Programme
on AMR containment in 2013, during the 12th (2012-2017) five-year plan which is being
coordinated by the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC). Under the programme, the
National AMR Surveillance Network (NARS-Net) has been established to monitor real time AMR
trends and to generate annual reports on National AMR Surveillance data obtained from NARS-
Net sites. The current report is the ninth annual report of AMR Surveillance data which includes

 The network sites are mandated to perform Internal quality control testing as per the
programme SOPs. 4 In addition, onsite support visits and trainings on data management are
conducted to strengthen bacteriology laboratory capacity, identify the challenges and improve
the quality of culture, identification and AST practices. The programme unit at NCDC also
frequently organizes workshops on use of WHONET AMR data management software to
facilitate timely AMR surveillance data flow from network sites to NCDC. Annual meetings to
review the performance of each site under NARS-Net are also conducted to discuss and resolve
site-specific challenges. This process plays a crucial role in strengthening and standardizing
antimicrobial resistance surveillance across the network.

 The WHONET 2024, an open-source offline microbiology data management desktop
application, has been used for collecting, collating and analyzing routine antimicrobial
susceptibility data generated by manual testing methods and automated systems at the
laboratories. In this report, M100 34th Ed. of Clinical & Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI)
guideline5 is used for the classification of the isolates as susceptible (S), intermediate (I), or
resistant (R). AMR data submitted monthly is reviewed during the monthly data quality
monitoring virtual calls conducted by the designated AMR nodal officer at NCDC for the
designated programme sites. The monthly data calls with the sites support them in validation
of data with respect to the completeness of data fields and compliance with the AMR
Surveillance panel of antibiotics. The errors observed in the data during data monitoring calls
are notified to the sites in the feedback emails. The subsequently received revised corrected
files are cleaned by NCDC nodal officers. A single file is generated from all the cumulative AMR
data files from each site and data de-duplication is done before carrying out the analysis.

### Source-grounded content

1.2.1. Data Deduplication

 For data analysis, only the first antibiotic susceptibility result has been considered for each
patient per specimen type and pathogen. For example, if two blood cultures from the same
patient yielded growth of E. coli, only the first has been included in the data; if the growth of E.
coli was detected in one culture and of K. pneumoniae in the other, both results have been
considered. If there was growth of E. coli in one blood culture and in one urine culture from the
same patient, both specimen types have been included. If for the same patient, multiple isolates
of same organism are included in the analysis, then there is a possibility that the data might get
skewed towards resistance especially for isolates like P.aeruginosa and A.baumanii. Therefore,
from each patient, only the first isolate of a given species from a particular specimen type isolated
during the surveillance period was included, regardless of its susceptibility profile.

 Deduplication of reported data of 2,17,513 isolates using WHONET revealed 2,02,573
unique patients. For the surveillance period, only one result has been considered for each patient
per specimen type and each pathogen. The deduplicated data file has been used for AST analysis.

1.2.2. Age and Gender distribution of reported AMR data

 Among 2,17,513 unique patients, AST data in this report is from 52.4% of male and
47.5% of female patients which is similar to the findings of last year (Fig 3). Majority of patients
were in the age category 35-64 years (39.8%) and 4.3% patients were in the age category 1-4
years. About 65.7 % patients were in the productive age group of 15-64 years. Figure 4
represents the distribution of priority bacterial pathogen isolates by age category.

 *Gender details were missing for 244 (0.1%) isolates

Figure 4: Distribution of priority pathogen isolates by age category (N=2,17,513)

 The analysis of 2025 AMR surveillance data revealed that the highest number of isolates
were from urine specimens (44.5%) (Table 2). The most commonly isolated priority bacterial
pathogen was E. coli (31%), which is similar to the previous five years, followed by Klebsiella
species (24%), Pseudomonas species (12%), S. aureus (11%), Acinetobacter species (10%)
Enterococcus species (10%) and Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi and Paratyphi (0.54%) (Table
3).

### Source-grounded content

E. coli (49%) was the most commonly isolated pathogen from urine specimens;
 Klebsiella species (25%) was the predominant isolate from blood specimens and from pus
 specimens Klebsiella spp (24%) and S. aureus (23%) were the predominant isolates. Among
 stool specimens, most common pathogen reported was Shigella species (46.6%), followed by
 Vibrio cholerae (41.3%), and Salmonella Typhi & Paratyphi (12.1%) (Table 3). Among the non-
 fermenting Gram-negative bacilli, Pseudomonas species was the most commonly isolated
 pathogen from pus aspirates (19%) and Acinetobacter species from blood culture specimens
 (23%) (Table 4). Amongst Gram-positive organisms, Enterococcus species was most the
 commonly isolated pathogen from urine specimens (68%) and S. aureus from pus aspirates
 (67%) (Table 4).

 In the 2025 AMR surveillance data, the majority of isolates (54%) were from patients

 outpatient clinics and 13% of the priority pathogens were isolated from Intensive care units
 (ICUs) (Fig. 5).

### Source-grounded content

1.2.3. AMR Surveillance of priority pathogens
1.2.3.1. Gram-Positive Cocci
 The AMR surveillance under NARS-Net covers the two most prevalent Gram-positive
bacterial human pathogens i.e., Staphylococcus aureus and Enterococcus species.

 Staphylococcus aureus

 During the 2025 reporting period, a total of 23,507 S. aureus isolates data was submitted
to NCDC (Table-3) constituting 11% of priority pathogens included in this annual report. AST
data analysis of 23,507 isolates revealed that majority of S. aureus were isolated from pus
specimens (67%). In this report, S. aureus was observed to be a significant cause of bacteremia
(29%) (Table 4).
 Approximately more than half of S. aureus isolated from blood (61%; 95% CI: 60.1-62.7)
were resistant to cefoxitin (a surrogate for mecA-mediated oxacillin resistance), while the
resistance to cefoxitin in pus aspirates (55%; 95% CI: 54.0-55.7) and other sterile body fluids
(55%; CI: 51.7-58.3) was lower in comparison to the blood isolates (Table 6). For analysis of
linezolid resistance in S. aureus, CLSI breakpoint for 2025 have been considered. Resistance to
Linezolid in S. aureus isolated from blood was found to be less than 1%, consistent with the
observations over last three years. Out of 14,833 isolates tested on Vancomycin screen agar,
no isolates showed growth on the vancomycin screen agar plate, hence no resistance was
observed to vancomycin.

Among the AMR Surveillance priority pathogens isolated in the data reporting period, S. aureus
was mainly isolated from inpatient wards followed by outpatient clinics and intensive care
settings (Table 5).

Among 11,090 isolates of MRSA all were sensitive to vancomycin and 7 isolates from blood
cultures were resistant to linezolid. All linezolid resistant isolates were confirmed at AMR-NRL
NCDC. Proportion of MRSA in blood has slightly increased from last year in all location settings,
from 63% to 65% in intensive care units, from 55% to 61% amongst inpatients and from 44% to
51% in outpatients (Fig. 7).

 Resistance to all the surveillance panel antibiotics was observed to be higher among

### Source-grounded content

Enterococcus species

 Enterococcus species isolates comprised of 10% of the annual AMR data and
contributed to 49% of the Gram-positive cocci data reported during 2025 (Table 3). A total of
22,318 Enterococcus species isolates data was submitted by the NARS-Net sites (Fig. 2). Upon
analysis, isolation rates from specimen types, namely urine, blood, pus aspirates and other
sterile body fluids were 68%, 17%, 10% and 5% respectively (Table 4). Among Enterococcus
species isolated from blood, highest resistance was observed to erythromycin 79% (CI: 77.8-
80.6) followed by Ampicillin (69%, CI: 67.0-70.3) (Table 7). Notably resistance to vancomycin
(30%, CI: 28.1-31.8) has increased from previous three years while the resistance to teicoplanin
(24%, CI: 22.0-25.2) has slightly decreased from last year (26%). Resistance to linezolid (2.6%,
CI: 2.0-3.2) has slightly increased among blood isolates from last year’s report (1.7%).

 Among the urinary isolates, 58% were resistant to first-line antibiotic ampicillin (CI: 56.7-
58.4) and 50% to gentamicin-high (CI: 48.7-58.4). Highest resistance was observed to
ciprofloxacin (81%, CI: 80.62-82.0) and lowest was observed to linezolid 0.7 % (CI: 0.6-0.8).
Resistance to vancomycin among urinary isolates has decreased to 9% in 2025 from 12% in
2024 (Table 7).

 Majority of Enterococcus spp. isolates were from patients in IPD followed by OPD and
ICU (Table 5). AST analysis of blood isolates of Enterococcus spp. showed low level resistance
to linezolid in isolates from patients from IPD, ICUs and OPD (Fig. 9). The incidence of VRE
among blood isolates was 20% in both inpatients and ICU settings which has slightly decreased
from the previous year (22%) (Fig. 9). Higher vancomycin resistance was observed in blood
isolates (30%) followed by other sterile body fluids, urine and pus aspirates (Fig. 9, 10). Among
urinary isolates of Enterococcus species, 45% resistance was observed to nitrofurantoin in ICU
settings.

### Source-grounded content

1.2.3.2. Gram-Negative Bacilli
 Seven Gram-Negative bacteria of public health importance are included under AMR
surveillance being coordinated at NARS-Net sites. These are Escherichia coli, Klebsiella species,
Pseudomonas species, Acinetobacter species, Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi and Paratyphi,
Shigella species and Vibrio cholerae.

1.2.3.2.1. Enterobacteriaceae
 Enterobacteriaceae accounted for 56% of all the priority pathogens.

 Escherichia coli

 E. coli (68,341) contributed to one-third of the total isolates data during the year 2025.
E coli was predominantly isolated from the urine specimens (69%) followed by pus aspirates
(21%), blood (6%) and other sterile body fluids (4%) respectively (Table 4).

E. coli isolates showed more than 50% resistance to all the tested antibiotics except
carbapenems, colistin and aminoglycosides. The highest resistance was observed to ampicillin
as noted in previous years (Table 8). High resistance to ciprofloxacin was observed ranging 73%
to 80% in all specimen types. Resistance to nitrofurantoin in urinary isolates showed an
increasing trend over last 4 years (increased from 9% in 2022 to 22% in 2025) (Table 8).

 Among third generation cephalosporins tested, resistance ranging between 79% to 85%
was observed in isolates from all specimen types. β-lactam-β-lactamase inhibitor combination
i.e. amoxicillin-clavulanate also had high resistance of 67% in blood isolates. Among
carbapenems, ertapenem (46%) had higher resistance than imipenem (39%) and meropenem
(38%) in E. coli blood isolates (Table 8). For colistin susceptibility testing, isolates were tested
using colistin agar dilution (ref: CLSI-M100 Ed. 35) and broth microdilution method, breakpoints
as per EUCAST guidelines were used. Among all the colistin resistant isolates submitted by the
NARS-Net sites, two isolates from blood (0.08%), one from OSBF (0.06%), two from pus
aspirates (0.02%) and thirteen from urine (0.05%) were confirmed as colistin resistant at AMR-
NRL, NCDC.

### Source-grounded content

Klebsiella species

 In the current data reporting period 52,597 isolates of Klebsiella species were reported.
The isolation of Klebsiella spp. in data reported by the sentinel sites was highest from urine
specimens (44%) followed by pus aspirate (31%), blood (18%) and OSBF (7%) (Table 4).

 Blood isolates showed more than 50% resistance to all tested antibiotics except for
colistin. ESBL producing Klebsiella species isolated from blood were higher (84%) in number
than from urine specimens (69%). Majority of carbapenemase producing Klebsiella species
were isolated from blood (58%-69%) followed by pus aspirates (46-53%), OSBF (46%-54%), and
urine specimens (36% - 42%). Forty five percent of the urinary isolates showed resistance to
aminoglycosides (amikacin and gentamycin); whereas more than half of the blood isolates were
resistant to aminoglycosides (amikacin; 63% and gentamicin; 56%) (Table 9). Approx. 58% of
urinary isolates showed resistance to nitrofurantoin.

 Resistance to the reserve antibiotic, colistin, was found to be highest in Klebsiella spp.
compared to other Gram-negative priority pathogens isolated from all the specimen types
which is similar to observations in previous year’s report. All colistin resistant isolates included
in this report have been confirmed at the AMR NRL at NCDC.

 Location type wise AST data revealed higher resistance to all the tested antibiotics in
Klebsiella species isolated from blood of ICU patients compared to the Klebsiella species
isolated from inpatients and outpatients (Fig. 13). Among carbapenems, ertapenem showed
highest resistance (72%) followed by meropenem (64%) and imipenem (64%) in blood isolates
from ICU patients. Similarly, high resistance was observed to third generation cephalosporins
viz. cefotaxime (86%), cefuroxime (87%) and ceftriaxone (87%) among blood isolates from
intensive care units.

### Source-grounded content

Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi and Paratyphi

 In the current reporting period, data of 1176 Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi and
Paratyphi isolates was submitted to NCDC. Thirty-one of these isolates were from stool
specimens and 1145 isolates were from blood. Among the first line antibiotics, highest
resistance was observed to ciprofloxacin (42%). Low resistance to other first-line antibiotics like
ampicillin (10%), chloramphenicol (6%) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (6%) was observed
(Table 10). Thirty-eight isolates of S. enterica serovar Typhi were found to be resistant to
ceftriaxone and sixteen isolates were resistant to azithromycin. Three isolates of ceftriaxone
resistant S. enterica serovar Paratyphi were observed during 2025. One isolate each of
Salmonella Typhi and Paratyphi A were found to be resistant to imipenem. All the ceftriaxone
resistant, azithromycin resistant and imipenem resistant S. Typhi isolates included in this report
were confirmed at the AMR-NRL at NCDC.

### Source-grounded content

1.2.3.2.2. Non-Fermenting Gram-Negative Bacilli

 Among the non-fermenting Gram-Negative bacilli (NF GNB) included in the data
submitted during January-December 2025 from the NARS-Net sentinel surveillance sites,
Pseudomonas species was the most frequently isolated pathogen from 26,637 isolates followed
by Acinetobacter species (22,711). Among the NF GNB, Pseudomonas species was the
predominant isolate from inpatients, while Acinetobacter species was the predominant isolate
from patients in ICU settings (Table 5).

 Pseudomonas species

 Pseudomonas spp. isolates included in the data during current reporting period were
most commonly isolated from pus aspirates (48%), urine (28%), blood (16%), and other sterile
body fluid (8%) specimens (Table 4).

 Blood culture isolates of Pseudomonas species showed highest resistance (37%; CI: 35.9-
38.9) to third-generation cephalosporin (ceftazidime) followed by amikacin (29%) 27.6-30.6,
ciprofloxacin (27%; CI: 26.0-28.9) and gentamicin (27%; CI: 25.0-28.3) amongst first line agents
for treating Pseudomonas species infections. Among pus aspirates, ceftazidime and
ciprofloxacin showed similar resistance i.e. 42% & 43% respectively. The resistance to
ceftazidime and ciprofloxacin in isolates from other sterile body fluids was 36% & 35%
respectively. Among the second line antibiotics, resistance to imipenem and aztreonam was
less than 40% (Table 12).

 Among urinary isolates, 54% Pseudomonas spp. isolates were resistant to ciprofloxacin,
53% to ceftazidime, 45% to gentamicin, 40% to aztreonam and 33% to piperacillin-tazobactam.
(Table 12). For the reserve group of antibiotic, namely colistin, twenty isolates from blood
cultures (0.7%), four from pus aspirate (0.1%) and four from urine (0.1%) were found to be
resistant (Table 12).

 Isolates of Pseudomonas spp. from blood cultures of patients in Intensive care units,
Inpatient and outpatient departments showed highest resistance to ceftazidime and aztreonam
among the tested antibiotics (Fig. 14). Among blood isolates from ICU patients, low resistance

Acinetobacter spp.

 Data of a total of 22,711 Acinetobacter species isolates were submitted by network sites
during this reporting period of Jan – Dec 2025. Among all specimen types included under the
programme, Acinetobacter species was most commonly isolated from blood (39%) followed by
pus aspirates (30%), urine (18%) and other sterile body fluid specimens (12%) (Table 4).

 High resistance was observed to all the tested antibiotics including Minocycline in
isolates from blood, pus specimens and other sterile body fluids in ICU patients (Fig. 15). Blood
isolates showed the highest resistance to ceftazidime (75%; CI: 74.2-76.2) followed by Imipenem
(70%; CI: 69.0-71.1). Alarmingly high level of resistance to second line antimicrobial agents viz.
imipenem (70%) and meropenem (67%) was observed among the blood isolates (Table 13).
Sixty-nine percent of isolates from pus specimens and 62% from other sterile body fluids were
resistant to imipenem. Twenty-five isolates from blood, two from OSBF, 7 from pus aspirates
and 4 isolates of urine were resistant to colistin (Table 13).

1.2.4. AMR Trends

 AMR Surveillance Data from NARSNET sites has been analyzed over last 8 years from 2017
to 2025. During 2020, data reported was small in volume due to the COVID pandemic. Trend
analysis of MRSA isolated from blood showed slight increase in MRSA proportion from 59%
(2021) to 61% (2025) (Fig. 16). This increase in proportion of MRSA may be attributed to the
increase in data volume as submitted by the network sites. Trend analysis of VRE isolated from
blood showed continuous increase from 2021 (11%) to 2025 (30%) (Fig. 18). Trend analysis for
ESBL producing E. coli isolated from blood showed an increase over the last 4 years from 2021
(76%) to 2024 (81%), in 2025 the trend is similar to the previous year (80%) (Fig. 19). The trends
observed for ESBL producing Klebsiella spp. from blood specimens showed consistently high
level of resistance ranging from 81% (2021) to 84% (2024) and in 2025 similar resistance level
was observed (83%) (Fig. 19). Four-year trend analysis of carbapenemase producing Klebsiella
species has shown consistent increase (Fig 21, 22). While for other organisms like E. coli,

1.2.3.2.3. Vibrionaceae

 Vibrio cholerae

In the current reporting period (Jan – Dec 2025), data of 106 isolates of Vibrio cholerae
confirmed at AMR-NRL has been analyzed. The highest resistance was observed to
trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and ampicillin i.e. 18% for both while no resistance to
chloramphenicol. All isolates were not tested to all surveillance panel antibiotics. (Table 14)

analysis of MRSA isolated from blood showed slight increase in MRSA proportion from 59%

increase in data volume as submitted by the network sites. Trend analysis of VRE isolated from

ESBL producing E. coli isolated from blood showed an increase over the last 4 years from 2021

1.2.5. Molecular Detection and Characterization of Priority Bacterial Pathogens

 Under the National Programme on Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) Containment, the
Antimicrobial Resistance National Reference Laboratory (AMR-NRL) for bacterial pathogens
established at the Centre for Bacterial Diseases and Drug Resistance Research (CBDDR),
National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), Delhi, received a total of 2,197 carbapenem-
resistant Gram-negative bacterial isolates and 170 vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus spp.
NARS-Net network sites for confirmation as a part of the External Quality Assurance Scheme
(EQAS) and as emerging AMR alerts.

 Among the 2,197 carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative isolates, 509 (23%) were
Escherichia coli, 744 (34%) were Klebsiella spp., 527 (24%) were Acinetobacter spp., and 417
(19%) were Pseudomonas spp. All isolates were confirmed at the AMR-NRL, CBDDR, NCDC using
standard biochemical identification methods and phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility
testing in accordance with established laboratory protocols.

 For molecular characterization of carbapenem resistance, 522 representative isolates
were randomly selected from different geographical regions of India, including North, South,
East, West, Central, and North-East India, to ensure regional representation. Conventional
polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was performed to detect the New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase
(NDM) and Oxacillinase-48 (OXA-48) carbapenemase genes. The selected isolates comprised
136 Escherichia coli, 152 Klebsiella spp., 136 Acinetobacter spp., and 98 Pseudomonas spp.

 For molecular characterization of vancomycin resistance, all 170 vancomycin-resistant
Enterococcus spp. received at the AMR-NRL, CBDDR, NCDC were analysed by conventional PCR
for the detection of the Vancomycin Resistance Gene Cluster A (vanA) and Vancomycin
Resistance Gene Cluster B (vanB) genes.

1.2.6. Discussion

 This report is the ninth annual report of the National AMR Surveillance Network (NARS-
Net). This report includes 2,17,513 isolates AST data submitted by 62 sites. Like the previous
year's findings, one-third of the pathogens in the AMR Surveillance data for 2025 were
Escherichia coli (31%). Among the urinary isolates, E. coli (44.5%) was the most commonly
isolated priority pathogen, and urine was the most common specimen type (45%). As
consistent with previous reports, S. aureus was most commonly isolated from pus aspirates
(67%). Klebsiella species was most commonly isolated pathogen from urine (44%) and pus
specimens (31%).

 Quality of AMR surveillance data submitted by the NARSNET sites has been ensured by
continuous hands-on laboratory and data management trainings, site support visits, monthly
data quality monitoring and feedback calls, and annual review meetings. EQAS program and
confirmation of AMR Alert isolates at AMR-NRL, CBDDR, NCDC also played an essential role in
improving data quality of NARS-Net sites. Moreover, many of the sites are strictly performing
internal quality control of media and antibiotic discs as per recommendations under the
programme.

 Compared to the previous year, the number of sites submitting data has increased from
54 to 62 sites situated in 34 states/UTs. Quality of colistin susceptibility testing has improved
over the years, as more than 50 sentinel sites have standardized and are performing colistin

### Source-grounded content

agar dilution and colistin broth microdilution (BMD) tests. The wet lab trainings on agar dilution
and broth microdilution are conducted on an annual basis as per need for NARS-Net sites.

 The AMR surveillance data in the current report like previous years continues to have
the limitation of samples for culture and sensitivity being referred only for patients requiring
admission and often not responding to the first line of antibiotics. This limitation has the
potential to skew the AMR trends to higher side than the actual trends.
Trend analysis over last 5 years for ESBL producing E. coli from blood has shown high prevalence
over the years (Fig. 19). This may be attributed to higher usage of third generation
cephalosporins for all the Gram-negative priority surveillance pathogens. High percentage of
resistance to third-generation cephalosporins and carbapenems in E. coli and Klebsiella species
and Acinetobacter species in India is a matter of concern. These findings highlight serious
challenges in treatment options for patients with infections caused by these priority bacterial
pathogens.

 There has been a gradual increase in the proportion of Vancomycin-resistant
Enterococcus (VRE) from blood specimens (from 11% in 2021 to 30% in 2025). (Fig. 18) Linezolid
resistance (2.6%) in blood isolates of Enterococcus species is slightly higher than that reported
last year. No Vancomycin-intermediate Staphylococcus aureus (VISA) or Vancomycin-resistant
Staphylococcus aureus (VRSA) has been reported over last 9 years. Trend analysis of MRSA
isolated from blood over the past 5 years shows a gradual increase to 61% in 2025. (Fig 16).
Among MRSA from blood specimens, highest resistance was observed to erythromycin (75%)
followed by ciprofloxacin (73%) and Clindamycin (48%) (Fig 8). The data of S. aureus continues
to be affected by the challenge of accurate identification of S. aureus using phenotypic methods
like hemolysis on sheep blood agar, slide coagulase and Mannitol Salt Agar.

 The AMR surveillance data presented in this report provides critical insights into
resistance trends and highlights areas needing focused attention. Strengthening surveillance
systems to generate quality AMR surveillance data, local use of data for generating
antibiograms to guide judicious use of antibiotics, strengthening infection prevention and
control in the health care facilities and the community to reduce infections and improving
awareness to promote behavior change towards judicious use of antibiotics are essential pillars
for AMR containment in the country. The findings in this report reinforce the value of
strengthening surveillance system and a unified national AMR network. Continued investment
in laboratory capacity, data quality, and site-level support is essential to build and maintain a
resilient national response to antimicrobial resistance.

### Source-grounded content

2. Fungal AMR Surveillance

2.1 Introduction

 The National Reference Laboratory (NRL) for Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in fungal
pathogens is established at Vallabhbhai Patel Chest Institute, New Delhi under the National
Programme on AMR Containment since September, 2021. As per the Global AMR Surveillance
System (GLASS) requirements, for surveillance of AMR in fungal pathogens, currently one fungal
pathogen genus that is Candida spp. from blood specimens is included. The National AMR
Surveillance network (NARSNet) sites under National Programme on AMR Containment
participating in the antifungal surveillance have been given wet-lab trainings on fungal
isolation, identification and antifungal sensitivity testing to build their capacity.

2.2 National Reference Laboratory for AMR in Fungal Pathogens

2.2.1 Participating laboratories and Candida strains processed at NRL for AMR
 surveillance
 The NRL at VPCI confirmed a total of 997 Candida spp. isolates from blood cultures from
39 NARSNet sites for phenotypic and molecular characterization and generation of antifungal
susceptibility profile under “National Programme on AMR Containment” from January 2025-
December 2025. List of NARS-Net sites participating for AMR surveillance in fungal pathogens
is at Annexure 1.

2.2.2 Methodology
 Phenotypic characterization of Candida isolates: All the stains received at NRL were
screened on differential selective media CHROMagarTM Candida Medium.
Molecular characterization: All strains were identified by Matrix-Assisted Laser
Desorption/Ionization Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometry (MALDI-TOF, Bruker Daltonics,
Bremen, Germany) and by sequencing of internal transcribed spacer region (ITS) of ribosomal
deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and of the D1/D2 domain of the large subunit ribosomal DNA in
case low or no identification was obtained by MALDI.
Antifungal susceptibility testing (AFST)
 Broth Microdilution Method: AFST was performed on 997 isolates using the Clinical and
Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) broth microdilution method (BMD) M27-A4, for
antifungals amphotericin B, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, 5-flucytosine,

2.2.3 Details of 997 yeasts characterized at NRL during 2025

Most common Candida species isolated from bloodstream infection were Candida tropicalis
(n=443, 45%) followed by Candida albicans (n=128, 13%), Candida parapsilosis (n=94, 10%),
Pichia kudriavzevii (n=81, 8%), Candida auris (n=43, 4%), Wickerhamomyces anomalus (n=43,
4%) and Cyberlindnera jadanii (n=32, 3%). Non-albicans Candida (NAC) species dominate the
distribution, highlighting the epidemiological shift from C. albicans.

2.2.3.1 Age and Gender distribution of isolates

 Overall, out of all the patients from whose blood culture specimens yeast strains were
isolated, 53% were male and 47% were female. Strikingly, neonates and infants (<1 year)
account for the majority of the isolates (50%), (Figure 3). Further, young adults (18-34 years)
accounted for 9% isolates and 11% were from middle aged (35-54 years) adults. The elderly
group (65 years and above) represented 5% of isolates. (Fig 30)

2.2.3.2 Location wise distribution of isolates

 The distribution of fungal isolates across healthcare settings show distinct patterns
among different yeast species (Table 16 17,18). Majority of the candidemia cases were from
the neonatal intensive care units (NICU) (23%), 5% were from the pediatric intensive care units
(PICU) (Table 18). Candida tropicalis and Candida albicans were the most commonly isolated
species. C. tropicalis being particularly prevalent in adult intensive care units (ICUs) (53%) and
inpatient departments (33%). Majority of isolates from inpatients departments were grown
from the blood specimens from pediatric and medicine wards. Candida albicans was most
commonly isolated from ICUs (47%), indicating its continued clinical significance in critical care.
(Table 16,17). Also, C. parapsilosis showed a strong presence in ICUs (54%). C. auris is a
multidrug-resistant species and was primarily found in ICUs (70%) followed by inpatient wards
(21%). Overall, ICUs accounted for the highest proportion of isolates for most species,
highlighting the critical care unit as a major reservoir for opportunistic fungal infections (Table
16).

 2.2.3.4 Antifungal Susceptibility testing

 Candida tropicalis: The azole susceptibility pattern of 443 C. tropicalis was assessed,
 fluconazole exhibited the highest resistance rate at approximately 6% (MIC, ≥8 mg/L), followed
 by voriconazole with a resistance of about 2.3% (MIC, ≥1 mg/L). Other antifungals like,
 itraconazole, posaconazole and amphotericin B, 5-fluorocytosine, micafungin, caspofungin,
 anidulafungin demonstrated good activity against all C. tropicalis isolates.

 Candida albicans: The resistance analysis of C. albicans (n=128) shows notable resistance to
 fluconazole (5.5%; MIC, ≥8 mg/L). Other azoles, echinocandins, 5-fluorocytosine and
 amphotericin B exhibited good activity against C. albicans isolates.

### Source-grounded content

Pichia kudriavzevii: The antifungal susceptibility pattern of P. kudriavzevii (n=81) reveals
intrinsic resistance to fluconazole (MIC >32mg/L).

Wickerhamomyces anomalus: As no breakpoints are available for W. anomalus, however
epidemiological cut-off values (ECV) are given in CLSI M57SEd.4, so we used ECV to categorise
the isolates into wild type and non-wild type. All strains (n=43) exhibited low MICs for all the
tested antifungals except fluconazole and amphotericin B. Out of 43, 4 isolates (9.3%) were
non-wild type as they exhibited MIC value >8 mg/L for fluconazole.

Candida auris: There are currently no established C. auris-specific susceptibility breakpoints in
CLSI-guidelines. Therefore, we use tentative breakpoints for C. auris against different
antifungals as recommended by CDC 2024. The antifungal susceptibility analysis of C. auris
(n=43) showed that 70% of the isolates were resistant to fluconazole (MIC, ≥32mg/L). Notably,
a small proportion of isolates (9.7%) shows high MIC value for amphotericin B (MIC, 4 mg/L).

bloodstream isolates, emphasizing the disproportionate burden of invasive fungal infections in
this vulnerable population. Consistent with this observation, almost 23% of all candidemia
cases originated from neonatal intensive care units (NICUs). The recovery of several uncommon
yeasts, including Cyberlindnera jadinii, Candida orthopsilosis, Clavispora lusitaniae, Candida
blankii, Diutina rugosa, and Trichosporon asahii, further demonstrates the diversity of invasive
yeast pathogens and highlights the importance of advanced identification methods such as
MALDI-TOF MS and ITS sequencing in routine surveillance. Antifungal susceptibility testing
demonstrated that azole resistance, particularly against fluconazole, remains the most
important resistance concern. The highest fluconazole resistance was observed in C. auris
(70%), Candida parapsilosis (19%) and Pichia kudriavzevii which is intrinsically resistant.
Resistance to amphotericin B, echinocandins, and other antifungal agents remained relatively
uncommon across most species, although reduced susceptibility was detected in a small
proportion of isolates, particularly among C. auris. These findings highlight the need for
continuous nationwide surveillance, accurate species-level identification, and routine
antifungal susceptibility testing to guide effective clinical management and antifungal
stewardship.
